title: Odd Lorentzian dimension: exactly one real form is split
text: Let $n$ be odd and consider the two real forms of the Lorentzian algebra in dimension $n$, $\Cl(1,n{-}1)$ (time of square $+1$) and $\Cl(n{-}1,1)$ (time of square $-1$). Then $\Cl(1,n{-}1)$ is type C if and only if $n \equiv 1 \pmod 4$, $\Cl(n{-}1,1)$ is type C if and only if $n \equiv 3 \pmod 4$, and in each case the other real form has complex type. The two real forms have the same complexification, which is split for every odd $n$: over $\C$ the element $\omega' = \omega$ or $i\omega$, whichever has square $+1$, is central, and $\tfrac12(1 \pm \omega')$ are its central idempotents. Thus the obstruction is present in every odd Lorentzian dimension; the real form decides whether it is visible as a splitting or hidden as a central complex structure.
proof: $\Cl(1,n{-}1)$ is the spacelike extension of $\Cl(1,n{-}2)$, an even-dimensional algebra with $p - q = 3 - n$, which is $\equiv 2 \pmod 4$ iff $n \equiv 1 \pmod 4$ and $\equiv 0$ iff $n \equiv 3$; Theorem \claimref{transport.where-obstruction-lies-commuting-square}(a) gives the first claim and the complex type of the other case. $\Cl(n{-}1,1)$ is the extension of $\Cl(n{-}2,1)$, $p - q = n - 3$, by a generator of square $+1$, obstructed iff $n - 3 \equiv 0$, i.e.\ $n \equiv 3 \pmod 4$, complex type otherwise. For the complexification: over $\C$ the substitution $e_i \mapsto ie_i$ on the generators of square $-1$ turns the relations of $\Cl(p,q)$ into those of $\Cl(n,0)$, so $\Cl(p,q) \otimes \C$ depends only on $n$ (\claimref{std-algebra.complexification}); the volume element remains central, and if $\omega^2 = -1$ then $(i\omega)^2 = +1$, so $\omega'$ as defined is a central involution and $\tfrac12(1 \pm \omega')$ are orthogonal central idempotents summing to $1$. The script checks the alternation, with its complex-type complement, in dimensions $3, 5, 7, 9, 11$.

title: Three dimensions
text: $n = 5$: $\Cl(1,4)$ is split, $\Cl(4,1)$ complex type. $n = 3$: $\Cl(2,1)$ is split, $\Cl(1,2)$ complex type. $n = 11$: $\Cl(10,1)$ is split, $\Cl(1,10)$ complex type. In the convention of this paper (time of square $+1$) the five-dimensional extension of spacetime is the split one; the planar and eleven-dimensional cases are split in the opposite convention. Physics done with complex gamma matrices sees the splitting in every odd dimension, as the corollary says it must; what the real form governs is the reality of the spinors.

title: Type P: the rule of no rule

text: This section gathers the results on type P: the rule of no rule. [[t]]
We turn to a further ingredient. [[t]]

title: Type P is self-repairing
text:
Let $A$ be any unital ring, $\mathcal{E}(A)$ its set of idempotents, and $A' \supseteq A$ any unital extension. The identity assignment
\[
\sigma : \mathcal{E}(A) \to A' , \qquad \sigma(e) = e,
\]
satisfies both von Neumann identities, $e\,\sigma(e)\,e = e$ and $\sigma(e)\,e\,\sigma(e) = \sigma(e)$, and is equivariant under \emph{every} ring automorphism of every extension: for any automorphism $\theta$ of $A'$ preserving $A$, $\sigma(\theta(e)) = \theta(\sigma(e))$ trivially. In the terminology of the taxonomy: the transport rule for type P is the identity, at signature increment $(0,0)$, and the repair is already present in the base algebra.
proof: $e\,e\,e = e^2 \cdot e = e \cdot e = e$, twice over; equivariance of the identity map is a tautology; and $\theta(e)$ is again an idempotent, so $\sigma$ is defined wherever equivariance asks it to be.

title: Why the shear has nothing to act on: $eee = e$ versus $vvv = 0$
text: The proposition looks too easy to be the analogue of Theorem \claimref{transport.no-go-level-elements}, so it is worth locating exactly where the difficulty of type N disappears. It is not in the shear, which is present on both sides: the pseudo-inverses of a null vector form a torsor under the null rotations (Proposition \claimref{transport.pseudo-inverse-torsor}), and the idempotents sharing the image of $e$ form one under $\mathrm{Hom}$-groups that the stabiliser of $e$ shears in exactly the same unipotent manner (Remark \claimref{note.transport.moore-penrose-boundary-idempotent-side} below). The difference is what the torsor contains. The null vector is not a member of its own repair family, since $v\,v\,v = 0 \neq v$, so equivariance must select from a set with no invariant point; the idempotent is a member of its own, since $eee = e$, so the repair need not lie in the sheared directions at all. One identity separates the two cases. The taxonomy's three transport costs, namely a hyperbolic plane for N (and even then only at the level of points), one generator for C, and nothing for P, are thus not a graded scale of difficulty but three different answers to the same equivariance question, each carrying its own theorem.
We turn to a further ingredient. [[t]]

title: Units span
text: In a finite-dimensional unital $\R$-algebra $A$, every element is a sum of two invertible elements.
proof: For $a \in A$ and $\lambda \in \R$, the element $a - \lambda 1$ is invertible iff the left-multiplication operator $L_a - \lambda\, \mathrm{id}$ on the finite-dimensional space $A$ is invertible (if $L_{a - \lambda 1}$ is bijective, the preimage of $1$ is a right inverse, and finite-dimensionality upgrades one-sided inverses to two-sided). The reals $\lambda$ for which $\det(L_a - \lambda\,\mathrm{id}) = 0$ are finitely many, so choose $\lambda$ with both $a - \lambda 1$ and $\lambda 1$ invertible ($\lambda \neq 0$): then $a = (a - \lambda 1) + \lambda 1$.

text: The next result builds directly on the one just stated. [[t]]

title: Classification of idempotent orbits
proof:
(1) Conjugation preserves rank, since $geg^{-1}$ has image $g(\mathrm{im}\, e)$. Conversely let $e, e'$ be idempotents of equal rank $r$ on $V = D^m$, on which $A \cong \Mat_m(D)$ acts (\claimref{transport.classification-real-clifford-algebras}). Each splits $V$: $V = \mathrm{im}\,e \oplus \ker e$, both summands free (a finitely generated submodule of a free module over a division ring is free, with well-defined dimension); choose $D$-bases of $\mathrm{im}\,e$ and $\ker e$, and likewise for $e'$. The $D$-linear map $g$ carrying the first adapted basis to the second is invertible and satisfies $g e g^{-1} = e'$, both sides being the projection onto $g(\mathrm{im}\,e) = \mathrm{im}\,e'$ along $g(\ker e) = \ker e'$. In the split case, invertible elements are pairs of invertibles and conjugation acts componentwise (inner automorphisms preserve the two ideals, which are the algebra's minimal central summands), so the same argument applies in each slot and no inner automorphism exchanges slots.

(2) is (1) applied to the pair, $\mathrm{rank}(1-e) = m - \mathrm{rank}(e)$.

(3) If $e$ is central its orbit is $\{e\}$. Conversely, if $geg^{-1} = e$ for every invertible $g$, then $e$ commutes with every invertible element, hence with every sum of two of them, hence with all of $A$ by Lemma \claimref{transport.units-span}: $e$ is central. The identification of the singleton-orbit idempotents with the taxonomy's type C, and of the moved ones with type P, is then Definition \claimref{obj.transport.obstruction-types} read against (1).

text: The next result builds directly on the one just stated. [[t]]

title: The pair is canonical; the label is a bit
text: For an idempotent $e \notin \{0,1\}$, set $u = 2e - 1$, an involution ($u^2 = 1$), with $e = \tfrac12(1+u)$ and $1 - e = \tfrac12(1-u)$ its spectral projections. The unordered pair $\{e, 1-e\}$ and the involution $\pm u$ determine one another canonically; the residual choice (which member to call $e$, equivalently the sign of $u$) is a $\mathbb{Z}_2$ labelling. By Theorem \claimref{transport.classification-idempotent-orbits}(2) this labelling is gauge (implemented by an inner automorphism) precisely for balanced pairs, and is canonically resolved by rank order otherwise. The pattern is now visible across the whole taxonomy: each obstruction type terminates in a residual $\mathbb{Z}_2$: the labelling of $\varepsilon_\pm$ for type C, exchangeable by no inner automorphism and rendered gauge only by the ascent (Proposition \claimref{transport.ascent-renders-grade-involution-inner}); the sign $\gamma$ of the fused ascent for Rule 2, not detected by the algebra (Remark \claimref{note.transport.bit-algebra-forgets}); and the labelling of $\{e, 1-e\}$ for type P, gauge already in the base algebra whenever the ranks permit. The three $\mathbb{Z}_2$'s are at strictly decreasing depth: outer, forgotten, inner.
proof: Everything except the last two sentences is contained in the displayed formulas and Theorem \claimref{transport.classification-idempotent-orbits}(2); the comparison across types collects Proposition \claimref{transport.ascent-renders-grade-involution-inner}, Remark \claimref{note.transport.bit-algebra-forgets} and Theorem \claimref{transport.classification-idempotent-orbits}(2), each proved where cited.

title: The Moore--Penrose boundary, idempotent side
text: One refinement of the type-P question does carry content, and it traces the boundary of the section ``The hyperbolic atom as a matrix algebra: the Moore--Penrose pseudoinverse'' from the other side. Within the idempotents sharing a fixed image $W$, is there a canonical one? They are in bijection with the complements of $W$, hence form a torsor under $\mathrm{Hom}(V/W, W)$ on which the stabiliser of $W$ acts by unipotent transvections, the same shear mechanism as the null rotations of Lemma \claimref{transport.group-null-rotations}. A definite Hermitian form resolves it, the orthogonal projection $P_W$ being the unique self-adjoint member; an indefinite one fails exactly on the degenerate subspaces, where no self-adjoint member exists at all: were $e$ self-adjoint with image $W$, any nonzero $z \in W \cap W^{\perp}$ would give $\langle x, z\rangle = \langle x, ez\rangle = \langle ex, z\rangle = 0$ for every $x$, against nondegeneracy of the ambient form. So the two sides agree: canonical selection is available exactly where a definite structure is. The transport-theoretic point is the division of labour. For type P the ambiguity concerns only \emph{which} idempotent to use, and the repair theorem needs no choice at all, since $\sigma(e) = e$ is asked about a given $e$; for type N the same ambiguity affects the repair itself, which is why the null cone needs the ascent and the idempotent variety does not.
We turn to a further ingredient. [[t]]

title: No fourth rule
text: The taxonomy of Definition \claimref{obj.transport.obstruction-types} is transport-complete with two nontrivial rules. Type N: ascend by one hyperbolic plane, with the repair delivered at the level of points (Theorems \claimref{transport.no-go-level-elements}, \claimref{transport.totality}, \claimref{transport.minimality}, \claimref{transport.representation-independent-minimality-completion}). Type C: ascend by one generator, with the fused algebra unique up to isomorphism (Theorems \claimref{transport.rule-2-ideal-fusion-sharp-form}, \claimref{transport.one-generator-minimal-minimal-completions-classified}, \claimref{transport.embedding-independent-minimality-fusion}). Type P: no ascent; the identity is an equivariant repair (Proposition \claimref{transport.type-p-self-repairing}). By the exhaustiveness theorem (Theorem \claimref{transport.exhaustiveness-every-zero-divisor-annihilated-idempotent}), every zero divisor of a nondegenerate real Clifford algebra falls under these three rules.

title: Rule 1 is Morita-trivial
text:
The elements
\[
E_{11} = ff^*, \qquad E_{22} = f^*f, \qquad E_{12} = f, \qquad E_{21} = f^*
\]
form a full $2 \times 2$ system of matrix units in $B$ ($E_{11} + E_{22} = 1$, $E_{ij}E_{kl} = \delta_{jk}E_{il}$); the corner is the base, $E_{11} B E_{11} = A\,ff^* \cong A$ via $a \mapsto a\,ff^*$; and therefore
\[
\Cl(p{+}1, q{+}1) \;\cong\; \Mat_2\bigl(\Cl(p,q)\bigr),
\]
under which the ascent embedding $A \hookrightarrow B$ becomes the twisted diagonal $a \mapsto \mathrm{diag}(a, \hat{a})$. In particular Rule 1 preserves the Morita class: the Wedderburn type, and with it the simplicity or splitness and the type-C diagnosis of the section ``A taxonomy of obstructions'', are the same for $B$ as for $A$, and the clock residue $d = p - q \pmod 8$ is fixed. (The \emph{presence} of types N and P is not preserved and could not be: Proposition \claimref{transport.no-transport-terminates} below shows every completion carries fresh obstructions of its own.) The adjoined ladder pair is, in the matrix description, exactly the off-diagonal matrix units, and the descent projectors $f^*f,\, ff^*$ are the diagonal ones.
proof: The matrix-unit relations are the hyperbolic-pair identities $v^2 = w^2 = 0, \qquad vw + wv = 1, \qquad \text{hence} \quad vwv = (1 - wv)v = v$ read off directly: $E_{12}E_{21} = ff^* = E_{11}$, $E_{21}E_{12} = f^*f = E_{22}$, $E_{12}^2 = f^2 = 0 = E_{21}^2$, $E_{11}E_{12} = ff^*f = f = E_{12}$, $E_{12}E_{11} = f\,ff^* = 0$, and so on; $E_{11} + E_{22} = 1$ is the pair's anticommutator. For the corner: using the displayed decomposition of $B$ and $ff^* a = a\, ff^*$ (evenness), one computes $ff^* (a_0 + a_1 f + a_2 f^* + a_3 ff^*)\, ff^* = (a_0 + a_3) ff^*$, since $ff^* \cdot f \cdot ff^* = f f^* Q(f) f^* = f \cdot ff^* = f^2 f^* = 0$ and likewise the $f^*$ term vanishes, while the $1$ and $ff^*$ terms remain; so $E_{11}BE_{11} = A\,ff^*$. The map $a \mapsto a\,ff^*$ is an algebra isomorphism onto it: multiplicative since $(a\,ff^*)(b\,ff^*) = ab\,(ff^*)^2 = ab\,ff^*$, unital onto the corner unit $ff^*$, injective by the directness of the decomposition. The Peirce isomorphism of Lemma \claimref{transport.matrix-units-peirce-isomorphism}, whose proof uses only the matrix-unit relations, then gives $B \cong \Mat_2(A)$. The embedding: for $a \in A$, $\varphi(a)_{11} = E_{11} a E_{11} = a\,ff^*$ and $\varphi(a)_{22} = E_{12}\, a\, E_{21} = f a f^* = \hat{a}\, ff^*$, while the off-diagonal entries vanish ($E_{11} a E_{21} = a\, ff^*f^* = 0$, $E_{12} a E_{11} = \hat a\,f ff^* = 0$); under the corner identification this is $\mathrm{diag}(a, \hat{a})$, which is multiplicative since the grade involution is an automorphism (\claimref{std-algebra.involution-properties}). Morita-class preservation, and with it the invariance of the type-C diagnosis, is the statement $\Mat_2(A) \sim_{\text{Morita}} A$ (\claimref{std-algebra.morita-amplification}) together with the fact that the Wedderburn data of $\Mat_2(\Mat_m(D))$ (or of the split case, blockwise) is that of $A$ with $m$ doubled.

title: Prior art, and what is new here
text: The isomorphism $\Cl(p{+}1,q{+}1) \cong \Mat_2(\Cl(p,q))$ is classical: it is the algebraic form of the $(1,1)$-periodicity of Clifford algebras \cite{ABS1964, Porteous1995, Lounesto2001}, usually obtained from $\Cl(p{+}1,q{+}1) \cong \Cl(p,q)\,\hat{\otimes}\,\Cl(1,1)$ and $\Cl(1,1) \cong \Mat_2(\R)$. What we claim as expository contribution is the presentation: the matrix units \emph{are} the transported ladder pair and its occupation projectors, so the periodicity isomorphism is not auxiliary to the transport principle but is the transport principle's own bookkeeping: the ascent adjoins exactly one row and column's worth of new structure, and the relations $f^2 = 0$, $ff^* + f^*f = 1$ are the matrix-unit relations of that adjunction. The parallel with Rule 2 is now exact (Remark \claimref{note.transport.2-pattern-two-rules-compared}): both rules amplify by $\Mat_2$, Rule 1 over the whole base, Rule 2 over its even half, and in both cases the matrix units are built from the completion's own canonical elements: the ladder pair for N, the central projectors plus the adjoined generator for C.

title: Iteration
text: Iterating Theorem \claimref{transport.rule-1-morita-trivial} gives $\Cl(p{+}k, q{+}k) \cong \Mat_{2^k}(\Cl(p,q))$: the tower over any base is Morita-stationary from its first step. The structural consequences of the iterated statement (tower rigidity, the one-mode-per-rung reading, and the direct limit) are the subject of the series' tower paper \cite{ButlerT3} and are not developed here.
The next result builds directly on the one just stated. [[t]]

title: Fusion occurs at most once
proof: (1) is Theorem \claimref{transport.rule-1-morita-trivial} and the count $d \mapsto d \pm 1$ for one adjoined generator. (2) is Theorem \claimref{transport.existence-classification-type-c} with the arithmetic $1 \pm 1 = 0, 2$ and $5 \pm 1 = 4, 6$ mod $8$. (3): once the residue leaves $\{1, 5\}$ it never returns, since Rule 1 fixes it and Rule 2 is only ever invoked (indeed only ever \emph{defined}, as a transport demand) at $\{1,5\}$; Morita-stationarity after the last (hence only) fusion is Theorem \claimref{transport.rule-1-morita-trivial} again. The closing statement on $\Cl(1,3)$ reads its residue $6$, simple and quaternionic, off \claimref{transport.classification-real-clifford-algebras}.

title: The pinching, and its kernel
text:
Define the pinching $E : B \to B$, $E(x) = PxP + (1-P)x(1-P)$. Then:
\begin{enumerate}
\item $E$ is an idempotent linear map whose image is the commutant $C = \{x \in B : xP = Px\} = A \oplus A\,ff^*$, on which it restricts to the identity, and $E$ is a $C$-bimodule map: $E(cxc') = c\,E(x)\,c'$ for $c, c' \in C$, with $E(1) = 1$: a conditional expectation onto $C$.
\item Its kernel is exactly the adjoined ladder sector:
\[
\ker E \;=\; PB(1-P) \,\oplus\, (1-P)BP \;=\; A f^* \,\oplus\, A f .
\]
In particular $E(f) = E(f^*) = 0$: the pinching erases precisely the pair the ascent adjoined, and nothing else.
\item The round trip is exact on transported elements: for $a \in A$, $E(a) = a$, and the corner read-out $D(x) = PxP$, identified with an $A$-valued map through the natural corner isomorphism $E_{22}BE_{22} = A\,f^*f \cong A$ ($a \mapsto a\,f^*f$), satisfies $D(a) = a$: ascent-then-descent is the \emph{identity} on the base. (In the Peirce coordinates of Theorem \claimref{transport.rule-1-morita-trivial}, which identify the $(2,2)$ block with the $(1,1)$ corner by conjugating with $E_{12} = f$, the same round trip reads as the grade involution $\hat{a}$; the two corner identifications differ by exactly the grade twist of the embedding $a \mapsto \mathrm{diag}(a,\hat a)$, and either way the map is an automorphism, faithful.) The multiplicative defect of $D$ on general elements is the exact interposition formula
\[
D(xy) - D(x)D(y) \;=\; P\,x\,(1-P)\,y\,P .
\]
\end{enumerate}
proof: (1) $E^2 = E$ and $E(1) = P + (1-P) = 1$ are immediate from $P^2 = P$. If $xP = Px$ then the cross-blocks of $x$ vanish ($Px(1-P) = xP(1-P) = 0$ and symmetrically), so $x = PxP + (1-P)x(1-P) = E(x)$; conversely $E(x)$ commutes with $P$ for any $x$; hence $\mathrm{im}\,E = C$ and $E|_C = \mathrm{id}$. The bimodule property follows by moving $c, c'$ through the projectors they commute with. The identification $C = A \oplus A\,ff^*$: $A$ commutes with $P$ (evenness of $f^*f$ in the $H$-factor) and so does $ff^*$, giving $A \oplus A\,ff^* \subseteq C$; and the two diagonal Peirce blocks $PBP \oplus (1-P)B(1-P) = A\,f^*f \oplus A\,ff^*$ span the same $2 \cdot 2^n$-dimensional space, since $a\,f^*f = a - a\,ff^*$. (2) The off-diagonal Peirce blocks contain $Af$ and $Af^*$ ($f = ff^*\cdot f = f \cdot f^*f$ places $f \in (1-P)BP$, symmetrically $f^* \in PB(1-P)$), and the dimensions ($2^n$ each, against Peirce blocks of dimension $2^n$ each in $\Mat_2(A)$) force equality. (3) $E(a) = a$ since $a \in C$. $D(a) = P a P = a\,f^*f$ (as $a$ commutes with $P$ and $P^2 = P$), which is $a$ under the natural corner isomorphism. The Peirce-coordinate reading: the $(2,2)$ entry of $\varphi(a)$ transported to the $E_{11}$ corner is $E_{12}\,a\,E_{21} = f a f^* = \hat{a}\,ff^*$, i.e.\ $\hat{a}$, as computed in Theorem \claimref{transport.rule-1-morita-trivial}. The defect formula is $D(xy) = Px(P + (1-P))yP = D(x)D(y) + Px(1-P)yP$.

title: The door is one-way
text: Let $A = \Cl(p,q)$ be nondegenerate and let $B$ be either minimal completion of this paper: the Rule-1 ascent $\Cl(p{+}1,q{+}1) \cong \Mat_2(A)$, or (when $p - q \equiv 1 \bmod 4$) a Rule-2 ascent $\cong \Mat_2(\Cl^0(p,q))$. Then there is no unital algebra homomorphism $B \to A$ whatsoever. Every descent is therefore non-multiplicative; the conditional expectation of Proposition \claimref{transport.pinching-kernel} is the canonical linear surrogate, and its loss, the erasure of the ladder sector, is forced by the algebra, not chosen by the formalism.
proof: $B$ is semisimple (\claimref{transport.classification-real-clifford-algebras}), so the kernel of a homomorphism $\theta : B \to A$ is a sum of Wedderburn blocks of $B$, and $\theta$ is injective on the complementary blocks; unitality ($\theta(1) = 1 \neq 0$) forces at least one block to survive. It suffices then that every block of $B$ has real dimension exceeding $\dim_\R A$. Rule 1, $A$ simple: $B \cong \Mat_2(A)$ (\claimref{transport.rule-1-morita-trivial}) is a single block of dimension $4 \dim A > \dim A$. Rule 1, $A = S \oplus S$ split: $\Mat_2(A) \cong \Mat_2(S) \oplus \Mat_2(S)$, blocks of dimension $4 \dim S = 2 \dim A > \dim A$. Rule 2 ($A$ split): $B \cong \Mat_2(\Cl^0)$ is simple (Theorem \claimref{transport.rule-2-ideal-fusion-sharp-form}) of dimension $2^{n+1} = 2\dim A > \dim A$. In every case no block embeds in $A$, contradiction.

title: The two-sided reading
text: Proposition \claimref{transport.pinching-kernel} and Theorem \claimref{transport.door-one-way} split the loose statement that descent is lossy into its two true halves. On transported elements the round trip is not lossy at all: it is the identity in the natural corner identification (the grade involution in Peirce coordinates; either way invertible), and the base algebra passes through the door unchanged in both directions. What cannot descend is the completion's \emph{new} content, the ladder pair and everything it generates off the diagonal, and this impossibility is a theorem about unital homomorphisms, not an artefact of choosing a particular descent map. The statement the computations support is sharper than the original: \emph{descent is invertible on the transported elements and impossible on the elements the ascent adjoined}. Compare the point-level statement of Lemma \claimref{transport.descent-read-out-map}: there the descent is exact on the whole invertible locus and fails only on the ideal points, which are precisely the values the ascent added. Element-level and point-level descent lose different things, and each loses exactly what its ascent supplied.

title: No transport terminates
text: No algebra reachable by a nonempty transport history is free of zero divisors. Every Rule-1 completion has mixed signature and so carries type N; indeed the adjoined pair $f, f^*$ is itself null: the repair of the old null cone is effected by adjoining new members of it. Every Rule-2 completion is a matrix algebra $\Mat_2(\Cl^0(p,q))$ and so carries type P: the fusion's own matrix units supply the non-central idempotents and nilpotents. Transport never reaches a division algebra; each completion carries fresh obstructions of its own.
proof: Rule 1 adjoins a hyperbolic plane, so the completed signature $(p{+}1, q{+}1)$ is mixed whatever the base, and Proposition \claimref{transport.existence-locus-type-n} applies; concretely $f^2 = 0$ with $f \neq 0$. Rule 2's completion contains the matrix units of Lemma \claimref{transport.matrix-units-peirce-isomorphism}: $E_{11}$ is a non-central idempotent (Theorem \claimref{transport.rule-2-ideal-fusion-sharp-form}(2)) and $E_{12}$ is a nonzero nilpotent.

title: Obstructions are moved, never destroyed
text: Proposition \claimref{transport.no-transport-terminates} is the zero-dimensional instance of a principle the transport programme repeatedly meets: a completion never removes degeneracy, it relocates it. We conjecture the following family form. For any family of quadratic forms degenerating tamely along a locus (in the sense of the series' sheaf-theoretic paper \cite{ButlerT4}), any completion of the family that is nondegenerate of constant signature on one side of the locus degenerates on a displaced locus on the other side; no completion is nondegenerate globally. The one-sided completion theorem and shadow wall of that paper prove exactly this for tame corank-one degenerations; the conjecture asserts the pattern is not an artefact of the tame case, and asks for the cohomological invariant that measures it, presumably a class built from the mod-8 residues on the two sides of the wall, the state machine of Proposition \claimref{transport.fusion-occurs-most-once} evaluated in families.

title: Transport
text: The \emph{transport} of a nondegenerate $(\mathbb{V}, Q)$ is the pair consisting of the minimal completion $\Cl(p{+}1,q{+}1)$ of Theorem \claimref{transport.minimality} and the null-ray representation $X(x) \;=\; \nO + x + \tfrac12 Q(x)\, \nInf$; the \emph{transported reciprocal} is the total involution $\iota$ of Theorem \claimref{transport.totality}. For a type-C obstruction the corresponding transport is the one-generator ascent of Theorem \claimref{transport.rule-2-ideal-fusion-sharp-form}; for type P it is the identity.

title: The transport algorithm
text:
The Principle says what is true; practice needs to know what to do. The theorems distil into a six-step procedure, and every step names the theorem, proved above, that licenses it. the table accompanying \claimref{transport.transport-algorithm} is the one-page version: the theorems in operational form. That the steps form a decision procedure with no gaps is itself a theorem, Corollary \claimref{transport.no-fourth-rule}.




\begin{enumerate}
\item[\textbf{Step 1.}] \textbf{Locate the failure.} Identify the element at which invertibility fails, or, if the construction is a family, the locus at which it fails. Nothing later depends on how this is done; it is a computation in the case at hand. What the algebra guarantees is that the failure cannot be argued away: a null vector has no inverse in \emph{any} unital algebra containing the base (Lemma \claimref{transport.noinverse}), and neither has an idempotent.

\item[\textbf{Step 2.}] \textbf{Diagnose the type.} Ask, in order:
  \begin{itemize}
  \item Is the failing element a vector $v$ with $Q(v) = 0$? Then the obstruction is \textbf{type N}. These exist exactly in mixed signature, $pq \neq 0$ (Proposition \claimref{transport.existence-locus-type-n}).
  \item Is it a \emph{central} idempotent? Then \textbf{type C}. These exist exactly when $p - q \equiv 1 \pmod 4$, and are then exactly the two projectors $\tfrac12(1 \pm \omega)$ (Theorem \claimref{transport.existence-classification-type-c}); equivalently, exactly when the algebra is not simple (Theorem \claimref{transport.classification-real-clifford-algebras}).
  \item Otherwise \textbf{type P}: a non-central idempotent, or an element annihilated by one.
  \end{itemize}
  The trichotomy is exhaustive: every zero divisor of a nondegenerate real Clifford algebra is annihilated by a nontrivial idempotent, possibly central in the split signatures, and then exactly when the element lies in one ideal (Theorem \claimref{transport.exhaustiveness-every-zero-divisor-annihilated-idempotent}). Two cautions. The nilpotency locus is strictly larger than the type-N locus, and nilpotence alone does not diagnose N (Example \claimref{note.transport.nilpotents-without-null-vectors-two-loci}); and a single algebra may carry all three types at once (Example \claimref{note.transport.cl-1-0-cl-2-1}).

\item[\textbf{Step 3.}] \textbf{Apply the rule.}
  \begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{Type N, Rule 1.} Adjoin one hyperbolic plane: $\Cl(p,q) \to \Cl(p{+}1,q{+}1)$. Do not expect the element to be repaired: no equivariant assignment of a partner to $v$ exists, in this ascent or any other (Theorem \claimref{transport.no-go-level-elements}), and the obstruction is a cohomology class that every enlargement pulls back unchanged (Theorem \claimref{transport.cohomological-form-no-go}). What is repaired is the space of points (Step 4). The increment is forced: $(+1,+1)$, never $(+2,0)$ or $(0,+2)$, among null-lift completions (Theorem \claimref{transport.minimality}), and no algebra with a smaller or differently balanced quadric can host the resolution however the base is embedded in it (Theorem \claimref{transport.representation-independent-minimality-completion}).
  \item \textbf{Type C, Rule 2.} Adjoin one generator $\nu$ orthogonal to $\mathbb{V}$, of either nonzero square. The grade involution becomes inner, the two ideals fuse, and the completion is $\Mat_2(\Cl^0(p,q))$, simple (Theorem \claimref{transport.rule-2-ideal-fusion-sharp-form}). The null-generator ascent is not an option: it produces a square-zero ideal and never fuses (Theorem \claimref{transport.one-generator-minimal-minimal-completions-classified}(2)). The sign of $\nu^2$ is free and the algebra forgets it (Remark \claimref{note.transport.bit-algebra-forgets}); if it matters for the application, it must be fixed by structure outside the algebra.
  \item \textbf{Type P.} Do nothing. The identity assignment $\sigma(e) = e$ is a total, fully equivariant von Neumann repair, at signature increment $(0,0)$ (Proposition \claimref{transport.type-p-self-repairing}).
  \end{itemize}

\item[\textbf{Step 4.}] \textbf{Compute in the completion.} For type N this is the substantive step, and it is where the classical formulas apply. Represent points, not elements: lift $x \in \mathbb{V}$ to the null ray of
  \[
  X(x) \;=\; \nO + x + \tfrac12 Q(x)\,\nInf ,
  \]
  which satisfies the incidence condition $Q(x) = 2st$ in the homogeneous coordinates $(s,x,t)$ of Proposition \claimref{transport.swap-rescale-normal-form}. The reciprocal is then the linear involution
  \[
  \iota(s,\,x,\,t) \;=\; (2t,\ x,\ \tfrac12 s),
  \]
  total on the quadric and never failing (Theorem \claimref{transport.totality}). All nonlinearity and all division have been deferred to a single read-out. This is the linearise-then-normalise pattern of homogeneous coordinates and M\"obius matrices, encountered here as forced rather than chosen (Remark \claimref{note.transport.classical}).

\item[\textbf{Step 5.}] \textbf{Descend, and state what descent costs.} Return the answer to $\mathbb{V}$ with the read-out $\dsc[\,s\nO + x + t\nInf\,] = x/s$. On the invertible locus the composite gives exactly the classical answer (Lemma \claimref{transport.descent-read-out-map}(2)); where the first slot vanishes the answer is an ideal point and corresponds to no point of $\mathbb{V}$ (Lemma \claimref{transport.descent-read-out-map}(3)). \emph{The refusal of the read-out is information, not failure}: it says the answer exists and lies outside the original space. At the level of elements the corresponding statement is stronger and worth knowing before relying on any descent: the pinching onto the base is a conditional expectation whose kernel is exactly the adjoined ladder sector (Proposition \claimref{transport.pinching-kernel}), and there is no unital algebra homomorphism from either completion back to its base at all (Theorem \claimref{transport.door-one-way}). Descent is invertible on the transported elements and impossible on the elements the ascent adjoined.

\item[\textbf{Step 6.}] \textbf{Iterate, or stop.} Ask whether the completion carries an obstruction of its own. It does: no transport terminates in a division algebra (Proposition \claimref{transport.no-transport-terminates}). But the bookkeeping is finite in the following sense: Rule 1 fixes the mod-8 residue, so the taxonomy of the completion is that of the base and iterating changes nothing structural (Theorem \claimref{transport.rule-1-morita-trivial}), while Rule 2 moves the residue off the split classes and can therefore occur at most once in any transport history (Proposition \claimref{transport.fusion-occurs-most-once}). A transport history takes at most one step on the clock, and then remains fixed.
\end{enumerate}

  total on the quadric and never failing (Theorem \claimref{transport.totality}). All nonlinearity and all division have been deferred to a single read-out. This is the linearise-then-normalise pattern of homogeneous coordinates and M\"obius matrices, encountered here as forced rather than chosen (Remark \claimref{note.transport.classical}).

\item[\textbf{Step 5.}] \textbf{Descend, and state what descent costs.} Return the answer to $\mathbb{V}$ with the read-out $\dsc[\,s\nO + x + t\nInf\,] = x/s$. On the invertible locus the composite gives exactly the classical answer (Lemma \claimref{transport.descent-read-out-map}(2)); where the first slot vanishes the answer is an ideal point and corresponds to no point of $\mathbb{V}$ (Lemma \claimref{transport.descent-read-out-map}(3)). \emph{The refusal of the read-out is information, not failure}: it says the answer exists and lies outside the original space. At the level of elements the corresponding statement is stronger and worth knowing before relying on any descent: the pinching onto the base is a conditional expectation whose kernel is exactly the adjoined ladder sector (Proposition \claimref{transport.pinching-kernel}), and there is no unital algebra homomorphism from either completion back to its base at all (Theorem \claimref{transport.door-one-way}). Descent is invertible on the transported elements and impossible on the elements the ascent adjoined.

\item[\textbf{Step 6.}] \textbf{Iterate, or stop.} Ask whether the completion carries an obstruction of its own. It does: no transport terminates in a division algebra (Proposition \claimref{transport.no-transport-terminates}). But the bookkeeping is finite in the following sense: Rule 1 fixes the mod-8 residue, so the taxonomy of the completion is that of the base and iterating changes nothing structural (Theorem \claimref{transport.rule-1-morita-trivial}), while Rule 2 moves the residue off the split classes and can therefore occur at most once in any transport history (Proposition \claimref{transport.fusion-occurs-most-once}). A transport history takes at most one step on the clock, and then remains fixed.
\end{enumerate}

title: A worked instance
text: The procedure is run end to end, on the case that motivated the programme, in the series' gravitational paper \cite{ButlerT5}, whose chain of steps mirrors the table accompanying \claimref{transport.transport-algorithm} row for row. It is worth carrying the outline through the paper as a running example. In it: the failure is located at the centre of the Schwarzschild solution, where the light cones fold onto a single direction (Step 1); the degenerating direction is null and the algebra $\Cl(1,3)$ is simple, with $d \equiv 6 \bmod 8$, so the diagnosis is type N and type C is unavailable (Step 2, by Theorem \claimref{transport.existence-classification-type-c} and Example \claimref{note.transport.cl-1-3-physical-case-n}); Rule 1 gives $\Cl(1,3) \to \Cl(2,4)$, the conformal algebra of spacetime, forced (Step 3); the transported division is total there (Step 4); and the descent is lossy in exactly the way Step 5 states, which is where that paper's physical content begins. The example is worth keeping in view for one reason in particular: the answer to the forbidden division is not a number in spacetime, and the algorithm says so in advance rather than after the fact.

title: What the procedure does not do
text:
Three boundaries, each a theorem rather than a caution.

It never returns an inverse. For type N no element-level repair exists at all (Theorem \claimref{transport.no-go-level-elements}); what the ascent supplies is a total operation on points together with a canonical destination for the values the base cannot hold. A reader who wants $1/v$ will not find it here, and Theorem \claimref{transport.no-go-level-elements} is the statement that nobody will.

It assumes the form is nondegenerate. Everything above is stated for nondegenerate $(\mathbb{V},Q)$. A degenerate form is not a harder case of the same problem but a different one: its radical generates a square-zero ideal rather than a resolvable obstruction (Theorem \claimref{transport.one-generator-minimal-minimal-completions-classified}(2) is the fibre-level instance), and completing it is the subject of the series' sheaf-theoretic paper \cite{ButlerT4}.

It is a procedure for one algebra. When division fails not at a point of an algebra but along a locus of a family, the rank of the relevant bundle cannot jump, and the correct object is a pair of sheaves rather than a single ascent: the fibrewise version of Step 3, with the completion performed over the degenerate locus and only there, is \cite[Thm.\ 4.4, Cor.\ 4.5]{ButlerT4}.

title: The centre
text: For $n \geq 1$, the centre of $\Cl(p,q)$ is $\R \cdot 1$ if $n$ is even, and $\R \cdot 1 \oplus \R \cdot \omega$ if $n$ is odd, where $\omega = e_1 e_2 \cdots e_n$ is the pseudoscalar.
provenance: Transport Lab claim primer.centre, version 2 (T00 Lem 9.4)

title: Classification of the real Clifford algebras
text: Let $d \equiv p - q \pmod 8$. Then $\Cl(p,q)$ is isomorphic, as a real associative algebra, to the entry of the table of the section ``The mod-8 classification'': $\Mat_k(\R)$ for $d \in \{0, 2\}$, $\Mat_k(\C)$ for $d \in \{3, 7\}$, $\Mat_k(\HH)$ for $d \in \{4, 6\}$, $\Mat_k(\R) \oplus \Mat_k(\R)$ for $d = 1$, and $\Mat_k(\HH) \oplus \Mat_k(\HH)$ for $d = 5$, with $k$ fixed in each case by $\dim_\R \Cl(p,q) = 2^n$. In particular $\Cl(p,q)$ is simple except when $p - q \equiv 1 \pmod 4$, where it is the direct sum of two isomorphic simple algebras.

title: The commutation rule
provenance: Transport Lab claim primer.commutation-rule, version 2 (T00 Lem 9.1)

title: The sign of $\omega^2$
text: $\displaystyle \omega^2 = (-1)^{\tfrac{n(n-1)}{2}} (-1)^q = (-1)^{\tfrac{(p-q)(p-q-1)}{2}}$. In particular $\omega^2 = +1$ if and only if $p - q \equiv 0$ or $1 \pmod 4$.
provenance: Transport Lab claim primer.sign, version 2 (T00 Lem 9.5)

title: Splitting along a hyperbolic plane
text:
Let $\mathbb{V}' = H_0 \perp U'$ be an orthogonal decomposition of a real quadratic space, with $H_0$ a hyperbolic plane spanned by a hyperbolic pair $(v, w_0)$ (a pair of null vectors with $v w_0 + w_0 v = 1$, Example \claimref{note.primer.hyperbolic-plane}); the form on $U'$ may be degenerate. Then:
\begin{enumerate}
\item $\{1, v, w_0, v w_0\}$ is a linear basis of $\Cl(H_0)$, and every element of $\Cl(\mathbb{V}')$ admits a \emph{unique} expansion
\[
\sigma \;=\; \alpha + v\beta + w_0\gamma + v w_0\,\delta, \qquad \alpha, \beta, \gamma, \delta \in \Cl(U').
\]
\item Left multiplication by $v$ is injective on $\Cl(U')$.
\end{enumerate}
provenance: Transport Lab claim primer.splitting-along-hyperbolic-plane, version 2 (T00 Lem 9.6)

title: The blade basis, degenerate forms included
text: Let $e_1, \dots, e_n$ be any basis of $V$. The $2^{n}$ ordered products $e_I = e_{i_1} e_{i_2} \cdots e_{i_k}$, for $I = \{i_1 < \dots < i_k\} \subseteq \{1, \dots, n\}$ (with $e_{\emptyset} = 1$), form a basis of $\Cl(V, Q)$. Hence $\dim \Cl(V, Q) = 2^{n}$, the map $\iota : V \to \Cl(V, Q)$ is injective, and $\Cl(V, Q) \ne 0$. This holds for every real quadratic space, degenerate or not.

title: Complexification, and the odd-dimensional split
The Clifford algebra exists and is unique
text: For every real quadratic space $(V, Q)$ a Clifford algebra exists: $\Cl(V, Q) = T(V) / I_Q$, the tensor algebra modulo the two-sided ideal generated by $\{v \otimes v - Q(v)\,1 : v \in V\}$, with $\iota$ the inclusion of $V = T^{1}(V)$ followed by the quotient map. Any two Clifford algebras of $(V, Q)$ are isomorphic by a unique isomorphism compatible with the maps from $V$. Concretely, for any real symmetric Gram matrix $G$ on $\R^{n}$ (degenerate allowed), the operators $c(v) = v \wedge {} + \, \iota_{Gv}$ on the exterior algebra $\Lambda \R^{n}$ satisfy $c(v)^{2} = Q(v)$, and so give a representation $\Cl(V, Q) \to \operatorname{End} \Lambda V$. (That this representation is faithful is shown afterwards, in the blade basis result, by the triangularity of $x \mapsto x \cdot 1$.)

title: The three involutions on each grade
An algebra and its matrix amplification
Orthogonal vectors anticommute
text: For $u, v \in V$: $u v = -v u$ if and only if $B(u, v) = 0$. In an orthogonal basis $e_1, \dots, e_n$, $e_i e_j = -e_j e_i$ for $i \ne j$ and $e_i^{2} = Q(e_i)$, and the product of two basis blades is $e_I e_J = \pm \bigl(\prod_{i \in I \cap J} Q(e_i)\bigr)\, e_{I \triangle J}$, the sign being $(-1)$ to the number of pairs $(i, j) \in I \times J$ with $i > j$.

title: Reflection in a non-null vector
Orthogonal bases and the law of inertia
text: Every real quadratic space $(V, Q)$ of dimension $n$ has an orthogonal basis $e_1, \dots, e_n$ with $Q(e_i) \in \{1, -1, 0\}$. The numbers $p$, $q$ and $r$ of basis vectors with $Q(e_i) = 1$, $-1$ and $0$ do not depend on the basis (Sylvester's law of inertia). Moreover $r = \dim \operatorname{rad} V$, and $p + q$ is the rank of any Gram matrix of $B$. Two real quadratic spaces are isometric if and only if they have the same $(p, q, r)$.
provenance: T. Y. Lam, Introduction to Quadratic Forms over Fields, AMS (2005)., the diagonalisation of forms and Sylvester's law of inertia (real case)

title: The product of two vectors
Hyperbolic pairs and the Witt decomposition
The even subalgebra and the Z2 grading
text: $\Cl(V, Q) = \Cl^{+} \oplus \Cl^{-}$ with $\Cl^{i} \Cl^{j} \subseteq \Cl^{i+j}$ (indices mod $2$). So $\Cl^{+}$ is a subalgebra, of dimension $2^{n-1}$ for $n \ge 1$, and $\Cl^{-}$ is a $\Cl^{+}$-bimodule. More finely, $\Cl^{j}\Cl^{k} \subseteq \bigoplus_{m} \Cl^{|j-k| + 2m}$, $0 \le m \le \min(j,k)$.

title: The two one-generator ascents differ as algebras
text:
Refuted. The conjecture was that the two one-generator ascents of a type-C algebra, adjoining $
u$ with $Q(
u) = +1$ or with $Q(
u) = -1$, are non-isomorphic algebras. The corrected statement is that the two ascents are always isomorphic as algebras; the sign of $Q(
u)$ is a geometric bit that the algebra forgets.

The transport results assemble into a six-step procedure (locate, diagnose, apply the rule, compute, descend, iterate) in which every step is licensed by a proved result and no case is left uncovered. [[c:transport.transport-algorithm]]
